label: thrm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thrm:main}
Let $d$ be a positive integer and $q$ a prime power. Then
$$
\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(q))=
\begin{cases}
d+1 & \textrm{when }(d,q)\ne(1,2),\\
1   & \textrm{when }(d,q)=(1,2).
\end{cases}
$$
Moreover,
$$
\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(q))=
\begin{cases}
d+2 & \textrm{when }q>2\textrm{ and }(d,q)\ne(1,3),\\
d+1 & \textrm{when }q=2\textrm{ and }d\textrm{ is odd},
      \textrm{ or when }(d,q)=(1,3),\\
d   & \textrm{when }q=2\textrm{ and }d\textrm{ is even},\\
                                 
\end{cases}
$$
Moreover, every subgroup of $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$ has relational complexity at most $d+2$ when $q>2$, and at most $d+1$ when $q=2$.
head: environment

label: thrm:main2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thrm:main2}
Let
$G=V\rtimes G_0\le \mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$,
where $G_0$ is the stabilizer in $G$ of the zero vector and acts irreducibly on $V$. Suppose that
$\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+2$.
Then $q>2$ and one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{part1} $d=1$ and $|G_0|>2$,
\item\label{part2} $d\ge 2$ and there exists a divisor $f_1$ of $f$ such that
\begin{align*}
&\mathrm{SL}_d(p^{f_1})\unlhd G_0
\le \mathrm{GL}_d(p^{f_1})\mathbb{F}_q^\ast,\\
&\mathrm{SL}_d(p^{f_1})<G_0\cap \mathrm{GL}_d(p^{f_1}),
\end{align*}
where $\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$ is identified with the group of non-zero scalar matrices in $\mathrm{GL}_d(q)$.

\item\label{part3} $d= 2$, $p=3$, $f$ is even and
$G_0=\mathrm{SL}_2(5)Z$, where $\mathrm{SL}_2(5)$ is a maximal subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2(9)$ and $Z\le\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$ is a group of scalar matrices. Moreover, $G_0$ contains a scalar matrix of order $4$.
\end{enumerate}


The converse also holds, that is, if $G_0$ is as in parts~\eqref{part1},~\eqref{part2} or~\eqref{part3}, then $G=V\rtimes G_0$ has relational complexity $d+2$.
head: environment

label: thrm:main3
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thrm:main3}
Let
$G=V\rtimes G_0\le \mathrm{AGL}_d(2)$,
where $G_0$ is the stabilizer in $G$ of the zero vector and acts irreducibly on $V$. Suppose that
$\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+1$.
Then one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{part12} $d$ is odd and $G_0=\mathrm{SL}_d(2)$,
\item\label{part22} $d\geq 2$ is even and $G_0$ is the natural image of either $\mathrm{Alt}(d+1)$ or $\mathrm{Alt}(d+2)$ acting on the fully deleted permutation module,
\item\label{part32} $d\ge 6$, $d$ is even and $G_0$ is either $\Omega_d^+(2)$ or $\Omega_d^-(2)$,
\item\label{part42} $d=4$ and $G_0=\mathrm{Alt}(7)$.
\end{enumerate}

The converse also holds, that is, if $G_0$ is as in parts~\eqref{part12},~\eqref{part22},~\eqref{part32} or~\eqref{part42}, then $G=V\rtimes G_0$ has relational complexity $d+1$.

label: l:0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:0}
Let $\emptyset\ne \Lambda\subseteq V$. Then $\Lambda$ is an independent set for the action of $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$ if and only if $\Lambda$ is a frame for some affine subspace of $V$, with the single exception that, when $(d,q)=(1,2)$, the frame $\Lambda=V$ is not independent.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $\Lambda$ is a frame for an affine subspace $\pi$ of $V$ and that $\Lambda\ne V$ when $(d,q)=(1,2)$. Up to replacing $\Lambda$ with a suitable $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$-conjugate, we have
$$
\Lambda=\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_\ell\}
$$
for some $0\le\ell\le d$. A direct calculation shows that the pointwise stabilizer of $\Lambda$ is strictly contained in the pointwise stabilizer of each subset obtained by deleting one point from $\Lambda$. Thus $\Lambda$ is an independent set for the action of $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$ on $V$.

Conversely, suppose that $\Lambda$ is an independent set for the action of $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$ on $V$. Up to replacing $\Lambda$ with a suitable $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$-conjugate, we may suppose that $0\in\Lambda$. Thus $\Lambda=\{0,v_1,\ldots,v_\ell\}$,
for some $v_1,\ldots,v_\ell\in V\setminus\{0\}$. It follows from the independence of $\Lambda$ that $\{v_1,\ldots,v_\ell\}$ is an independent set for the action of $\mathrm{GL}_d(q)$ on $V$. Hence the vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_\ell$ are linearly independent. Therefore, $\Lambda$ is a frame for the affine subspace
$$
0+\langle v_1,\ldots,v_\ell\rangle.
$$
Finally, when $(d,q)=(1,2)$, the pointwise stabilizers of $V$ and of either singleton subset of $V$ are all trivial, so $V$ is not independent.

label: l: almost independent
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l: almost independent}
Suppose that $m$ is a positive integer, that $I,J\in \Omega^{m+1}$, that $I\sim_{m} J$ but $I\not\sim_{m+1} J$. Then the underlying set of $I$ (and, therefore, of $J$) is an almost independent set.
head: environment

label: l:aiodd
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:aiodd}
Suppose that $q>2$, and let $\Lambda$ be an almost independent subset of $V$ of cardinality at least $d+2$. Then $|\Lambda|=d+2$, and $\Lambda$ is $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$-conjugate to a set of the form
$$
\left\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d,\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i e_i\right\},
$$
where $\alpha_i\ne 0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i\ne 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, the set $\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}$ is independent. By Lemma~\ref{l:0}, it has cardinality at most $d+1$. Therefore,
$|\Lambda|\le d+2$,
and hence $|\Lambda|=d+2$.

Fix $\lambda\in\Lambda$. The set $\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}$ is a frame for $V$. After replacing $\Lambda$ by a suitable $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$-conjugate, we may assume that
$$
\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}=\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}.
$$
Write 
$\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i e_i$.
The result now follows from the observation preceding the lemma.
head: environment

label: l:ai
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:aiodd}, we have
$|\Lambda|\le d+2$.

Suppose first that $|\Lambda|=d+1$. If $\Lambda$ is independent, then by Lemma~\ref{l:0} it is a frame for $V$ and is therefore conjugate to the set in~\eqref{l:ai1}.

Suppose that $\Lambda$ is not independent. Choose $\lambda\in\Lambda$. Since $\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}$ is an independent set of cardinality $d$, it is a frame for an affine subspace of dimension $d-1$. After replacing $\Lambda$ by a suitable conjugate, we may assume that
$$
\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}
=
\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}\}.
$$
Since $\Lambda$ is not independent, $\lambda$ belongs to the affine span of these points. Thus
$$
\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\alpha_i e_i.
$$
The observation preceding Lemma~\ref{l:aiodd} shows that every $\alpha_i$ is non-zero and that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\alpha_i\ne 1.
$$
Since $q=2$, we have $\alpha_i=1$ for every $i$. The second condition is therefore equivalent to $d-1$ being even, or equivalently to $d$ being odd. This gives the set in~\eqref{l:ai2}.

Suppose now that $|\Lambda|=d+2$. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:aiodd}, we may assume that
$$
\Lambda=
\left\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d,
\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i e_i\right\}.
$$
Once again, every $\alpha_i$ is non-zero, and hence $\alpha_i=1$ for every $i$. Moreover,
$$
\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i\ne 1
$$
if and only if $d$ is even. This gives the set in~\eqref{l:ai3}.
head: environment

label: l:binarysubgroups
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The case $d=1$ is immediate, so assume $d\ge 2$.
Suppose that there exist $I$ and $J$ with $I\sim_{d+1}J$ and $I\not\sim_{d+2}J$. By Lemma~\ref{l: almost independent}, we may assume that the underlying sets $I'$ and $J'$ of $I$ and $J$ are almost independent sets of cardinality $d+2$. These sets are also almost independent sets for $\mathrm{AGL}_d(2)$ and hence, by Lemma~\ref{l:ai}, we have that $d$ is even and $I=(P_0,\ldots,P_d,P_{d+1})$ and $J=(Q_0,\ldots,Q_d,Q_{d+1})$, where $\{P_0,\ldots,P_d\}$ and $\{Q_0,\ldots,Q_d\}$ are frames and $P_{d+1}=\sum_iP_i$ and $Q_{d+1}=\sum_iQ_i$. Since $I\sim_{d+1}J$, we may assume $P_i=Q_i,$ for every $i\in \{0,\ldots,d\}$. Over the field with two elements, this implies $P_{d+1}=Q_{d+1}$ and $I=J$, contrary to the fact that $I\not\sim_{d+2}J$.
head: environment

label: eq:q+2
title: Proof
body_md:
The formula for the height follows from Lemma~\ref{l:0}. Indeed, a frame of an affine subspace of dimension $\ell$ has cardinality $\ell+1$, and the largest affine subspaces of $V$ have dimension $d$. The exceptional case $(d,q)=(1,2)$ also follows from Lemma~\ref{l:0}.

It follows from~\eqref{eq:2.1} that
$\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(q))\le d+2$
when $(d,q)\ne(1,2)$. When $(d,q)=(1,2)$, we have
$\mathrm{AGL}_1(2)=\mathrm{Sym}(2)$,
and hence
$\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_1(2))=2$.
Similarly, when $(d,q)=(1,3)$, we have
$\mathrm{AGL}_1(3)=\mathrm{Sym}(3)$,
and hence 
$\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_1(3))=2$.

Assume now that $q>2$ and $(d,q)\ne(1,3)$. For
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_d)\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\ast)^d$,
define
$$
T(a)=
\left(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d,\sum_{i=1}^d a_i e_i\right).
$$
Suppose that $a,b\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\ast)^d$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q+2}
\sum_{i=1}^d a_i\ne 1,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^d b_i\ne 1,
\qquad
a\ne b.
\end{equation}
We claim that
\[
T(a)\sim_{d+1}T(b) \textrm{  and  }
T(a)\not\sim_{d+2}T(b). \]

To prove the claim, observe first that, after deleting the last entry, the two tuples are identical. After deleting $e_i$, the remaining points form a frame for $V$ in each tuple because $a_i$ and $b_i$ are non-zero. After deleting $0$, the remaining points form a frame for $V$ because
$\sum_{i=1}^d a_i\ne 1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^d b_i\ne 1$.
Thus, since $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$ is transitive on ordered frames we deduce that $T(a)\sim_{d+1}T(b)$.
On the other hand, an element mapping $T(a)$ to $T(b)$ would fix
$0,e_1,\ldots,e_d$
and would therefore be the identity. This is impossible because $a\ne b$. Hence
$T(a)\not\sim_{d+2}T(b)$, as claimed. 

The claim implies that, so long as there exist $a,b$ satisfying~\eqref{eq:q+2}, we have $\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(q))=d+2$. It remains to show that such $a$ and $b$ exist.

Suppose first that $q>3$. Choose $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$ such that
$d\alpha\ne 1$.
Then choose
$\lambda\notin
\{0,\alpha,1-(d-1)\alpha\}$.
Such choices are possible because $q>3$. We may now take
$a=(\alpha,\ldots,\alpha)$
and $b=(\lambda,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha)$.

It remains to consider $q=3$ and $d>1$. If $d\equiv2\pmod 3$, take
$a=(1,\ldots,1)$
and $b=(-1,1,\ldots,1)$.
If $d\equiv0\pmod 3$, take 
$a=(-1,\ldots,-1)$
and
$b=(1,-1,\ldots,-1)$.
Finally, if $d\equiv1\pmod 3$ and $d\ge4$, take
$a=(-1,\ldots,-1)$
and
$b=(1,1,-1,\ldots,-1)$.
In each case, all coordinates are non-zero, the coordinate sums are not equal to $1$, and $a\ne b$. Therefore,
$\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(q))=d+2$
whenever $q>2$ and $(d,q)\ne(1,3)$.

Assume now that $q=2$ and $d>1$.                     
                                 
                             
                
                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                     
   
                                                  
   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                
                                            
Suppose first that $d$ is odd and $d>1$. Consider the two $(d+1)$-tuples
\begin{align*}
I&=(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d),\\
J&=\left(0,e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1},
\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}e_i\right).
\end{align*}
                                                                                  
$I\not\sim_{d+1}J$.
We claim that 
$I\sim_d J$.
After deleting the last entry, the two tuples are identical. After deleting any $e_i$ with $1\le i\le d-1$, the remaining points form frames for affine subspaces of dimension $d-1$. Finally, after deleting $0$, the remaining points again form frames for affine subspaces of dimension $d-1$, because $d-1$ is even. Hence
$I\sim_d J$.
It follows that
$\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(2))=d+1$
when $d>1$ is odd by Lemma~\ref{l:binarysubgroups}.

Finally, suppose that $d$ is even. We first prove that
$\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(2))\ge d$.
When $d=2$, this is vacuous, so suppose that $d\ge4$. Consider the two $d$-tuples
\begin{align*}
I&=(0,e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}),\\
J&=\left(0,e_1,\ldots,e_{d-2},
\sum_{i=1}^{d-2}e_i\right).
\end{align*}
The entries of $I$ form a frame for an affine subspace of dimension $d-1$, whereas the entries of $J$ do not. Thus
$I\not\sim_d J$.
The same deletion argument used in the odd-dimensional case shows that
$I\sim_{d-1}J$,
because $d-2$ is even. Therefore,
$\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(2))\ge d$.

It remains to prove the reverse inequality. Let $I,J\in V^{d+1}$ satisfy
$I\sim_d J$.
By Lemmas~\ref{l: almost independent} and~\ref{l:binarysubgroups}, it is enough to consider the case in which the sets of entries of $I$ and $J$ are almost independent and have cardinality $d+1$.
Since $d$ is even, Lemma~\ref{l:ai} shows that both sets of entries are frames for $V$. The regular action of $\mathrm{AGL}_d(2)$ on ordered frames therefore gives
 $I\sim_{d+1}J$.
Hence $
\mathrm{RC}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(2))\le d$.

We finish with the only assumption on $(d,q)$ being that it is not in $\{(1,2),(1,3)\}$.  Let $K$ be a subgroup of $\mathrm{AGL}_d(q)$. Then, from~\eqref{eq:2.1} and from the monotonicity of the height function, $\mathrm{RC}(K)\le \mathrm{H}(K)+1\le \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{AGL}_d(q))+1=d+2$. By Lemma~\ref{l:binarysubgroups}, the stronger inequality $\mathrm{RC}(K)\le d+1$ holds when $q=2$. This concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref{thrm:main}.

label: l:irredN
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:irredN}
    Let $\mathbb{F}_{q_0}\leq \mathbb{F}_q$ be an inclusion of fields. Let $E\leq H$ be the group of all matrices of the form $I_d+w^\top\delta$ where $w$ ranges over $W:=\langle X\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{q_0}}$ for some $X\subseteq V$ and $\delta$ is a fixed non-zero row vector. Suppose that the common fixed-point space $C_V(E)=\mathbb{F}_q\delta$, and that $H\geq E$ is irreducible on $V$. Then $N:=\langle E^g\mid g\in H\rangle$ is irreducible on $V$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $0\ne U\le V$ be an $N$-invariant subspace. In particular, $U$ is $E$-invariant. Suppose first that there exist $x\in U$ and $u\in W$ such that $xu^\top\ne 0$. Then
$$
x(I_d+u^\top\delta)-x=(xu^\top)\delta\in U,
$$
and hence
$$
\mathbb{F}_q\delta\le U.
$$
On the other hand, if $xu^\top=0$ for every $x\in U$ and every $u\in W$, then
$$
U\le {\bf C}_V(E)=\mathbb{F}_q\delta.
$$
Since $U\ne 0$, we again obtain $
\mathbb{F}_q\delta\le U$.
Since $U$ is $N$-invariant, it is invariant under $E^g$ for every $g\in H$. Applying the preceding argument to each $E^g$, we obtain
$\mathbb{F}_q\delta^g\le U,$
for every $g\in H$. Since $H$ acts irreducibly on $V$ and $\delta\ne 0$, we have
$$
V=\sum_{g\in H}\mathbb{F}_q\delta^g.
$$
Therefore, $U=V$, and $N$ is irreducible.

label: l:d=1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:d=1}
    Suppose that $d=1$. Then $\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+2=3$ if and only if $|G_0|>2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $|G_0|>2$. Choose $
\gamma\in G_0\setminus\{1,-1\}$,
and set
$$
\alpha=\frac{1}{1+\gamma},
\qquad
\beta=\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma}.
$$
Consider the triples
$I=(0,1,\alpha)$ and 
$J=(0,1,\beta)$.
The pairs obtained by deleting the third entries are identical. The map
$$
x\longmapsto \gamma x
$$
maps $(0,\alpha)$ to $(0,\beta)$, while the map
$$
x\longmapsto \gamma^{-1}x+1-\gamma^{-1}
$$
maps $(1,\alpha)$ to $(1,\beta)$. Since $\gamma,\gamma^{-1}\in G_0$, it follows that
$I\sim_2J$.
On the other hand, $\alpha\ne\beta$, because $\gamma\ne1$, and the only affine transformation fixing both $0$ and $1$ is the identity. Hence
$I\not\sim_3J$.
Therefore, $\mathrm{RC}(G)\ge3$. Since $\mathrm{H}(G)\le \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{AGL}_1(q))=2$ by Theorem~\ref{thrm:main},
equation~\eqref{eq:2.1} gives $\mathrm{RC}(G)\le3$. Thus $\mathrm{RC}(G)=3$.

Conversely, suppose that $|G_0|\le2$. If $|G_0|=1$ then $G$ is regular, hence $\mathrm{RC}(G)=2$. Suppose that $|G_0|=2$. Then $2\mid (q-1)$, so $q$ is odd and we have
$G_0=\{1,-1\}$.
Let $$I=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\sim_2(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=J$$
be $2$-equivalent tuples. If all entries of $I$ are equal, then all entries of $J$ are equal, and a translation maps $I$ to $J$. Otherwise, choose $r,s$ such that $x_r\ne x_s$. After applying an element of $G$ to $J$, we may assume that
$y_r=x_r$ and $y_s=x_s$.
For every $k\leq n$, since $I\sim_2 J$ we deduce that there is some $(u,\ell)\in\mathbb{F}_q\rtimes\{1,-1\}$ such that $$(u+\ell x_r,u+\ell x_k)=(x_r,x_k)^{(u,\ell)}=(y_r,y_k)=(x_r,y_k).$$ In particular, $y_k-x_r=u+\ell x_k-u-\ell x_r=\ell(x_k-x_r)$, that is, for every $k\leq n$, $y_k-x_r=\pm(x_k-x_r)$ and similarly $y_k-x_s=\pm(x_k-x_s)$.
If $y_k\ne x_k$, the first equality gives $y_k=2x_r-x_k$,
while the second gives $y_k=2x_s-x_k$.
Since the characteristic is odd, this implies $x_r=x_s$, a contradiction. Therefore, $y_k=x_k$ for every $k$, and hence $I\sim_nJ$. Thus $\mathrm{RC}(G)=2$.

label: l:Bidef
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:Bidef}
    Let $i\in \{1,\dots,d\}$, and let $\delta$, $c_i$ and $B_i$ be defined as above. Then $$B_i=I_d+c_i\delta$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $(0,e_1,\dots,e_{i-1},e_{i+1},\dots,e_d,v)$ and $(0,e_1,\dots,e_{i-1},e_{i+1},\dots,e_d,w)$ are ordered frames, it suffices to show that $I_d+c_i\delta$ maps $v$ to $w$ and fixes $e_j$ for every $j\ne i$.

    Let $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}\setminus\{i\}$. Then $$e_j(I_d+c_i\delta)=e_j+\frac{1}{\alpha_i}e_je_i^\top \delta=e_j+0,$$ as desired. Moreover, $$v(I_d+c_i\delta)=v+\frac{1}{\alpha_i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^d\alpha_je_j\right)e_i^\top \delta=v+\delta=w,$$ as was to be shown.
head: environment

label: l:B0def
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:Bidef}, it suffices to show that $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\delta+e_i(I_d+c_0\delta)=e_i$ for each $i\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ and that $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\delta+v(I_d+c_0\delta)=w$.

    Let $i\in\{1,\dots,d\}$. Then $(e_ic_0)\delta=-\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\delta$, whence $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\delta+e_i(I_d+c_0\delta)=e_i$. Additionally, $vc_0=-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}$, so $$\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\delta+v(I_d+c_0\delta)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\delta+v-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\delta=\delta+v=w,$$ as was to be shown.

title: Lemma
body_md: The group $K$ contains an elementary abelian group $E=\{I_d+u\delta\mid u\in W\}$ of transvections of dimension $d-1$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q_0}$. Moreover, the common fixed-point space of $E$ on $V$ is $\mathbf{C}_V(E)=\mathbb{F}_q\delta$. Set $N:=\langle E^g\mid g\in G_0\rangle$. Then $N\trianglelefteq G_0$, $N\leq \mathrm{SL}_d(q)$, and $N$ is irreducible.

label: eq:key
title: Proof
body_md:
Throughout this proof we will repeatedly use that $\lambda_j-1=\delta c_j$ for $j\in\{0,\dots, d\}$. This implies first that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:key}
\delta u_j=(\lambda_j-1)\delta c_r -(\lambda_r-1)\delta c_j=(\delta c_j)\delta c_r -(\delta c_r)\delta c_j=0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for any $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, 
\[B_j^{-1}=(I_d+c_j\delta)^{-1}=I_d-\dfrac{c_j\delta}{\lambda_j}.\]
Therefore, for $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\setminus\{r\}$,
\[
(B_jB_r)^{-1}=\left(I_d-\dfrac{c_r\delta}{\lambda_r}\right)\left(I_d-\dfrac{c_j\delta}{\lambda_j}\right)=I_d-\frac{c_r\delta}{\lambda_r}-\frac{c_j\delta}{\lambda_j}+\frac{c_r\delta c_j\delta}{\lambda_r\lambda_j}= I_d-\frac{c_j\delta}{\lambda_j}-\frac{c_r\delta}{\lambda_r\lambda_j},\]
where the final equality is using (again) that $\delta c_j=\lambda_j-1$. Similarly, \[B_rB_j=(I_d+c_r\delta)(I_d+c_j\delta)=I_d+c_r\delta+c_j\delta+(\lambda_j-1)c_r\delta=I_d+\lambda_jc_r\delta+c_j\delta, 
\]
whence
\begin{align*}(B_jB_r)^{-1}B_rB_j&=\left(I_d-\frac{c_j\delta}{\lambda_j}-\frac{c_r\delta}{\lambda_r\lambda_j}\right)(I_d+\lambda_jc_r\delta+c_j\delta)\\&=I_d-\frac{c_j\delta}{\lambda_j}-\frac{c_r\delta}{\lambda_r\lambda_j}+\lambda_jc_r\delta-c_j\delta c_r\delta-\frac{c_r\delta c_r\delta}{\lambda_r}+c_j\delta-\frac{c_j\delta c_j\delta}{\lambda_j}-\frac{c_r\delta c_j\delta}{\lambda_r\lambda_j}\\&=
I_d-c_r\delta+\lambda_jc_r\delta-(\lambda_r-1)c_j\delta\\&=I_d+u_j\delta.\end{align*}

By~\eqref{eq:key},
$
(u_j\delta)^2=0,
$
thus, for $j\ne r$ the element $I_d+u_j\delta$ is a transvection in $K$.

The vectors $u_j$, with $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\setminus\{r\}$, are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_{q_0}$. Indeed, the vectors $c_1,\ldots,c_d$ form an $\mathbb{F}_q$-basis of the column-vector space, and, in any linear combination of the $u_j$, the coefficient of $c_j$ is $-(\lambda_r-1)$ times the coefficient of $u_j$.

If $u$ is a column vector satisfying $\delta u=0$, then 
$$
B_i^{-1}(I_d+u\delta)B_i=(I_d-\lambda_i^{-1}c_i\delta)(I_d+u\delta)(I_d+c_i\delta)=(I_d+u\delta-\lambda_i^{-1}c_i\delta)(I_d+c_i\delta)=I_d+\lambda_i u\delta.
$$
Also, if $\delta u=\delta u'=0$, then
$$
(I_d+u\delta)(I_d+u'\delta)=I_d+(u+u')\delta.
$$
It follows that $K$ contains $E$. Moreover, $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q_0}}(W)=d-1$, $|E|=q_0^{d-1}$,
and every nonidentity element of $E$ is a transvection in $K$, and hence in $G_0$: products add the parameters $u$, while conjugation by $B_i$
multiplies them by $\lambda_i$; thus the admissible scalars contain $\mathbb{F}_{q_0}$. We have now proved the first claim.

Observe next that
$$
\mathbb{F}_qW
=
\ker(\delta),
$$
where by abuse of notation we are identifying with $\delta$ the linear mapping $V^\top \to \mathbb{F}_q$ sending $u$ to $\delta u$. Given vectors $u,v\in V$, $v$ is fixed by $I+u^\top\delta$ if and only if $vu^\top=0$, whence the common fixed-point space of $E$ is (isomorphic to) the annihilator of $\mathbb{F}_q W=\ker(\delta)$, and hence has dimension 1 over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Therefore, 
$$
{\bf C}_V(E)=\mathbb{F}_q\delta.
$$

Clearly $N=\langle E^g\mid g\in G_0\rangle\unlhd G_0$ and $N\le \mathrm{SL}_d(q)$---that $N$ is irreducible follows from Lemma~\ref{l:irredN}.
head: environment

label: l:noforms
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:noforms}
    Suppose that $d\geq3$. Then $N$ preserves no nondegenerate alternating, Hermitian, or quadratic form.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose otherwise. If $x$ is a transvection in $E$ preserving such a form and $[V_1,x]=L_1$, then $
{\bf C}_{V_1}(x)=L_1^\perp$.
Since every nonidentity element of $E$ has moved line $L_1$, it follows
that
${\bf C}_{V_1}(E)=L_1^\perp$.
On the other hand, we have seen above that $
{\bf C}_{V_1}(E)=L_1$.
Thus $L_1=L_1^\perp$.
This is impossible when $d\ge3$, because 
$\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q_1}}L_1=1$
whereas
$\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q_1}}L_1^\perp=d-1>1$.
Therefore the unitary, symplectic, and orthogonal cases do not occur
when $d\ge3$.
head: environment

label: l:d=2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:d=2}
    If $N\ne \mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)$, then $d=2$ and $N$ is either a classical group in characteristic $p$ or $q_1=9$ and $N\cong \mathrm{SL}_2(5)\leq \mathrm{GL}_2(9).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider first the monomial case~\eqref{case5}, that is
$$
N\cong C_a^{d-1}\rtimes\mathrm{Sym}(d)
$$
in its natural monomial representation. Since $a$ is odd, a
transvection in $N$ has permutation part consisting of a single
transposition. After permuting the basis, its non-trivial block has the
form
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
0&c\\
c^{-1}&0
\end{pmatrix}
$$
for some $c\in\mathbb{F}_{q_1}^\ast$. Its moved line is
$$
\left\langle e_i+ce_j\right\rangle.
$$
The moved line determines the pair $\{i,j\}$ and the scalar $c$, and
hence determines the transvection. Thus there is at most one
transvection in $N$ with any prescribed moved line.

All nonidentity elements of $E$ have the same moved line. Therefore
$E$ has at most one nonidentity element, and hence $|E|\le 2$.
This is impossible. Indeed, the monomial case occurs only in
characteristic $2$, and~\eqref{lambdar} implies that
$\mathbb{F}_{q_0}\ne\mathbb{F}_2$.
Consequently, $q_0\ge4$ and $|E|=q_0^{d-1}\ge4$.
Thus the monomial case cannot occur.

We now exclude case~\eqref{case6}. A group of this type preserves
a nondegenerate alternating form on its fully deleted permutation module;
see~\cite[Section~6.2]{Eberhard}. Hence, we may assume that $d=2$ by Lemma~\ref{l:noforms}. Since $d=2$, the image of the symmetric group on the fully deleted permutation
module is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}_2(2)$ and has Sylow $2$-subgroups
of order $2$. This is also impossible, since in characteristic $2$ we
have $|E|=q_0\ge4$. Similarly, a dihedral group of order dividing $2(q_1+1)$ has Sylow 2-subgroup of order $2$, so case~\eqref{case10} cannot occur.


Consider now case~\eqref{case8}.
This case has characteristic $2$. Since $q_0\ge4$ and $d=3$, we have
$|E|=q_0^2\ge4^2=16$.
However, a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $3.A_6$ has order $8$.
Therefore $3.A_6$ cannot contain $E$, and this case is
impossible.

Consider now case~\eqref{case9}.
Again the characteristic is $2$, and $|E|=q_0^5\ge4^5=2^{10}$.
On the other hand, a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $3.\mathrm{P}\Omega_{6}^{-,\pi}(3)$
has cardinality $2^8$.
Thus this group cannot contain $E$, and this case is also impossible.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: If $N$ is a classical group in characteristic $p$ then $N=\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{l:noforms}, we can assume that $d=2$. Now, 
$\mathrm{Sp}_2(q_1)=\mathrm{SL}_2(q_1)$,
so the symplectic case is already the linear case. Moreover, if
$q_1=s^2$, then the natural group $\mathrm{SU}_2(s)$ is conjugate in
$\mathrm{GL}_2(q_1)$ to $\mathrm{SL}_2(s)$. It is therefore contained
in a proper subfield subgroup, contrary to the minimality of $q_1$.
The two-dimensional orthogonal case can occur only in characteristic
$2$. In that case, $
|\mathrm{O}_2^\pm(q_1)|=2(q_1\mp1)$,
so every Sylow $2$-subgroup has order $2$. Since $|E|\ge4$, this case
is also impossible.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Suppose that $N=\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)$. Then
$\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)\unlhd G_0
\le \mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$, and\\
$\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)<G_0\cap \mathrm{GL}_d(q_1),$ where $\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$ is identified with the group of scalar matrices.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After conjugation in $\mathrm{GL}_d(q)$,
$
N=\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)\unlhd G_0.
$
Therefore
$$
G_0\le
{\bf N}_{\mathrm{GL}_d(q)}
\bigl(\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)\bigr)=\mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)\mathbb{F}_q^\ast.
$$
                                                   
   
                           
                               
  
                                     
   
Hence
$
\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)\unlhd G_0
\le
\mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$.
                                                                   

Next, we may write $B_r=\lambda B$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$ and $B\in\mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)$. Since each of the $B_i$ have the same moved line $L$ over $V$, it follows that $B$ preserves $L_1$ as defined in~\eqref{eq:L1}. Additionally, we have already seen that $B_r$ acts trivially on $V/L$, whence $B$ acts as the scalar $\lambda^{-1}$ on $V/L$ and hence on $V_1/L_1$. Thus, $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q_1}^\ast$, and so $B_r\in\mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)$. Moreover, $\det(B_r)=\lambda_r\ne1$, so $\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)<G_0\cap \mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)$.
head: environment

label: eq:normalizer
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\overline{g}\in\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)$ centralize $\overline{N}$, and
choose $g\in\mathrm{GL}_2(q)$ with $\pi(g)=\overline{g}$. For every
$n\in N$, there exists $\lambda_n\in\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$ such that
$g^{-1}ng=\lambda_n n$.
The map
$n\longmapsto\lambda_n$
is a homomorphism from $N$ to $\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$. Since
$N\cong\mathrm{SL}_2(5)$ is perfect, this homomorphism is trivial.
Therefore, $g^{-1}ng=n$
for every $n\in N$.
Now, the natural two-dimensional representation of $N$ is absolutely
irreducible. Indeed, if it were reducible over the algebraic closure, then $N$ would be conjugate to a subgroup of the group of upper
triangular matrices, which is solvable. This is impossible because
$N\cong\mathrm{SL}_2(5)$ is not solvable. Hence, by Schur's lemma,
$${\bf C}_{\mathrm{GL}_2(q)}(N)=\mathbb{F}_q^\ast.$$
Thus $g$ is scalar and $\overline{g}=1$, proving that
${\bf C}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})=1$.
Conjugation now gives an embedding
$$
{\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})
\longrightarrow
\mathrm{Aut}(\overline{N})\cong \mathrm{Sym}(5).
$$
Since the image contains the group of inner automorphisms
$\mathrm{Inn}(\overline{N})\cong \mathrm{Alt}(5)$,
we have
${\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})
\cong \mathrm{Alt}(5)$ or ${\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})
\cong \mathrm{Sym}(5)$. If the first possibility occurs, then $\bar N={\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline N)$ and our claim is proven. Thus
suppose, for a contradiction, that
${\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})\cong \mathrm{Sym}(5)$.
Choose a subfield
$\mathbb{F}_{3^m}\le\mathbb{F}_q$
of smallest possible order such that, after conjugation,
$$
{\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})
\le\mathrm{PGL}_2(3^m).
$$
Since this group contains $\overline{N}\cong \mathrm{Alt}(5)$, we have $m\ge2$.
Let $M$ be a maximal subgroup of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(3^m)$ containing
${\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})$.  By Dickson's classification~\cite{Giudici},
$\mathrm{PSL}_2(3^m)$ has no subgroup isomorphic to
$\mathrm{Sym}(5)$. Hence
${\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})
\not\le \mathrm{PSL}_2(3^m)$, and therefore $M$ does not contain
$\mathrm{PSL}_2(3^m)$.



By~\cite[Theorem~3.5]{Giudici} (see also~\cite{Dickson}), $M$ is one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item a point stabilizer;
\item a dihedral group;
\item a subgroup isomorphic to $S_4$;
\item a proper subfield subgroup $\mathrm{PGL}_2(3^{m_0})$.
\end{enumerate}
The first two possibilities are solvable, and the third has order $24$,
so none of them can contain a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathrm{Sym}(5)$. The final
possibility contradicts the minimality of $m$. Therefore,
${\bf N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2(q)}(\overline{N})
\not\cong \mathrm{Sym}(5).$ Hence the result.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Suppose that $p=3$ and that $N=\mathrm{SL}_2(5)<\mathrm{SL}_2(9)$. Then $G_0=NZ$ where $Z\leq\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$, and $G_0$ contains a scalar matrix of order 4.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, observe that Lemma~\ref{eq:normalizer} implies that $
{\bf N}_{\mathrm{GL}_2(q)}(N)=N\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$.
Set $Z=G_0\cap \mathbb{F}_q^\ast$. Since $N\unlhd G_0$, we have
$G_0=ZN$. 

It remains to show that $G_0$ contains a scalar matrix of order $4$. Since $K\leq G_0=ZN$ we have that
$B_0,B_1,B_2$ are three distinct non-scalar elements of $G_0$, all having the
same moved line $L=\mathbb{F}_q\delta$.

Let $\overline{B}_i$ denote the projective image of $B_i$. Since
$G_0/Z\cong \mathrm{Alt}(5)$,
the order of each $\overline{B}_i$ is $2$, $3$, or $5$.
We claim that at least one $\overline{B}_i$ has order $2$. Suppose
otherwise.
If some $\overline{B}_i$ has order 3, then $$B_i^3=(I_d+c_i\delta)^3=I_d+(c_i\delta)^3=I_d+(\delta c_i)^2c_i\delta\in\mathbb{F}_q^\ast,$$ since we are working in characteristic 3. But $c_i\delta$ has rank 1, and thus $\delta c_i=0$, that is, $B_i$ is a transvection. Thus, if all three projective images have order $3$, then each $B_i$ is a
transvection belonging to $N$. The transvections in $N$ with moved
line $L$, together with the identity, form a $3$-subgroup of $N$.
Since a Sylow $3$-subgroup of $N$ has order $3$,
there are at most two nonidentity transvections in $N$ with moved line
$L$. This contradicts the fact that $B_0,B_1,B_2$ are distinct.

Suppose that some $\overline{B}_i$ has order $3$ and some
$\overline{B}_j$ has order $5$. Then $
\langle\overline{B}_i,\overline{B}_j\rangle$
fixes $L$ and is therefore a proper subgroup of $\mathrm{Alt}(5)$. However, no
proper subgroup of $\mathrm{Alt}(5)$ contains elements of both orders $3$ and $5$,
a contradiction.

Finally, suppose that all three projective images have order $5$.
Since they generate a proper subgroup of $\mathrm{Alt}(5)$ fixing $L$, they belong
to the same cyclic subgroup of order $5$. Consequently, $B_0,B_1$ and $B_2$  all fix setwise the same two lines.  It follows that the rank-one
matrices $
B_i-I_2=c_i\delta$
have the same kernel, and hence the vectors $c_0,c_1,c_2$ are proportional.
This contradicts the linear independence of $c_1$ and $c_2$ -- see~\eqref{def:ci}.

Thus some $\overline{B}_i$ has order $2$. Write $
B_i=zn$,
with $zI_2\in Z$ and $n\in N$. Since $B_i$ has an eigenvalue $1$ and its
projective image has order $2$, its other eigenvalue is $-1$. Therefore,
$\det(B_i)=-1$.
On the other hand,  $\det(B_i)=z^2$,
because $n\in\mathrm{SL}_2(q)$. Hence 
$z^2=-1$.
Thus $zI_2$ has order $4$ and belongs to $G_0$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Suppose that $d\ge 2$ and that there exists a divisor $f_1$ of $f$ such that $\mathrm{SL}_d(p^{f_1})\unlhd G_0
\le \mathrm{GL}_d(p^{f_1})\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$, and
$\mathrm{SL}_d(p^{f_1})<G_0\cap \mathrm{GL}_d(p^{f_1})$. Then $\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $q_1=p^{f_1}$, let  $H_1=G_0\cap\mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)$ 
and  $D=\det(H_1)\leq\mathbb{F}_{q_1}^\ast$.
Since
$$
\ker\left(
\det:\mathrm{GL}_d(q_1)\longrightarrow
\mathbb{F}_{q_1}^\ast
\right)
=
\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)
$$
and $\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)<H_1$,
we have $H_1 =\left\{
A\in\mathrm{GL}_d(q_1):
\det(A)\in D
\right\}$.The strict inclusion $\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)<H_1$
implies that $D\neq\{1\}$ and, in particular, $q_1>2$. Choose 
$\lambda\in D$ with
$\lambda\neq1$. Next, choose non-zero $\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_d\in\mathbb{F}_{q_1}^\ast$ with $\sum_{i=2}^d\gamma_i=1$. The existence of $\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_d$ is guaranteed by the fact that $q_1>2$.
Define $z=\sum_{i=2}^d\gamma_i e_i$, $v=e_1+z$ and
$w=\lambda e_1+z$.
By construction, all coordinates  of $v$ and $w$ are non-zero, the sum of the coordinates is not $1$ and $v\neq w$. In particular,~\eqref{eq:condition1} and~\eqref{eq:condition2} are satisfied.

Let $\delta=w-v$, $I=(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d,v)$ and $J=(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d,w)$. Consider the matrices $B_1,\ldots,B_d$ in Lemma~\ref{l:Bidef} and the matrix $B_0$ in Lemma~\ref{l:B0def}.

From~\eqref{eq:det1}, for $0\leq i\leq d$, we have
$$
\det(B_i)=
\begin{cases}
\lambda&\textrm{when }i\in\{0,1\},\\
1&\textrm{when }i>1.
\end{cases}
$$
All entries of the matrices \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_d\) belong to
\(\mathbb{F}_{q_1}\). Hence
$$
B_0,B_1\in H_1
$$
because their determinants belong to $D$, while
$$
B_2,\ldots,B_d\in\mathrm{SL}_d(q_1)\leq H_1.
$$

Therefore $
B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_d\in G_0.$ Similar calculations to the proofs of Lemmas~\ref{l:Bidef} and~\ref{l:B0def} show that $I\sim_{d+1}J$ whereas clearly $I\not\sim_{d+2}J$ since $v\ne w$. Hence $\mathrm{RC}(V\rtimes G_0)\ge d+2$. The reverse inequality follows
from Theorem~\ref{thrm:main}, and therefore
$\mathrm{RC}(V\rtimes G_0)=d+2$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Suppose that $d= 2$, $p=3$, $f$ is even and that
$G_0=NZ$, where $N=\mathrm{SL}_2(5)$ is a maximal subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2(9)$ and $Z\le\mathbb{F}_q^\ast$ is a group of scalar matrices containing an element of order $4$. Then $\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+2=4.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathbb{F}_9\le\mathbb{F}_q$, we may choose $\iota\in\mathbb{F}_9$ such that
$\iota^2=-1$
and $\iota I_2\in G_0$.
Let $
\overline{N}=N/\{\pm I_2\}\cong \mathrm{Alt}(5)$.
Choose an element $\overline{t}\in\overline{N}$ of order $3$. The normalizer of $\langle\overline{t}\rangle$ in $\overline{N}$
is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Sym}(3)$. So there exists an
involution $\overline{x}\in\overline{N}$ such that
$\overline{x}\,\overline{t}\,\overline{x}^{-1}
=
\overline{t}^{-1}$.
Choose lifts $t,x\in N$ such that $t$ has order $3$. Then $t$ is a
transvection, while
$x^2=-I_2$ and $x^{-1}tx=t^{-1}$.

After choosing a suitable basis $e_1,e_2$ of $V$, we may assume that
$$
t=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
1&1
\end{pmatrix}
\hbox{ and }
x=
\iota
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&0\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Define
$$
B_1=\iota^{-1}x=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&0\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_2=t=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
1&1
\end{pmatrix},
$$
and
$$
B_0=B_1B_2=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&0\\
1&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Since $\iota I_2\in G_0$ and $x,t\in N$, all three matrices belong to
$G_0$.

Now set $
v=e_1+e_2$ and $w=-e_1+e_2$.
Then
$v\ne w$,
and a direct calculation gives
$$
(0,e_2,v)^{B_1}=(0,e_2,w)
$$
and
$$
(0,e_1,v)^{B_2}=(0,e_1,w).
$$
Moreover, the affine transformation
$
(-e_1,B_0)
$
satisfies
$
(e_1,e_2,v)^{(-e_1,B_0)}
=
(e_1,e_2,w).
$
Thus $(0,e_1,e_2,v)\sim_3(0,e_1,e_2,w)$ and $(0,e_1,e_2,v)\not\sim_4(0,e_1,e_2,w)$. Hence $\mathrm{RC}(G)\ge4$. The reverse inequality follows from
Theorem~\ref{thrm:main}, and therefore $\mathrm{RC}(G)=4$.

label: thrm:calculations
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: l:formpres
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:formpres}
    Suppose that $d\geq 4$. Let $\langle\, , \rangle$ denote the natural nondegenerate alternating or polar form on $V$ preserved by $G_0$. Then $U=\delta^\perp$, where orthogonality is with respect to the form $\langle\, , \rangle$. Therefore, $\langle e_d,\delta\rangle=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $j\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$. Since $d\geq4$, we may choose $i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}\setminus\{j\}$.
The matrix $B_i$ fixes $e_j$ and maps
$e_d$ to $w=e_d+\delta$.
Since $B_i$ preserves the form,
\[
\langle e_j,e_d\rangle
=
\langle e_jB_i,e_dB_i\rangle
=
\langle e_j,e_d+\delta\rangle.
\]
It follows that $\langle e_j,\delta\rangle=0$.
This holds for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$, and hence $U\leq\delta^\perp$.
Since $\delta\neq0$ and the form is nondegenerate,
$\dim\delta^\perp=d-1$.
As $\dim U=d-1$, we obtain $U=\delta^\perp$, as claimed.
In particular, $e_d\notin\delta^\perp$, and hence $\langle e_d,\delta\rangle=1$.

label: l:non-singular-basis
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:non-singular-basis}
Let $(V,Q)$ be a nondegenerate orthogonal space of even dimension $d$
over $\mathbb F_2$. Suppose either that $V$ has minus type, or that
$V$ has plus type and $d\geq6$. Then $V$ has a basis
$f_1,\ldots,f_d$ such that
$Q(f_i)=1$, for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$ and
$Q(f_1+\cdots+f_d)=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $p$ denote the associated polar form. We first describe a four-dimensional plus-type space which will be
used to increase the dimension by $4$. Let
$P=\langle \alpha,\beta\rangle\perp\langle \gamma,\delta\rangle$,
where $(\alpha,\beta)$ and $(\gamma,\delta)$ are hyperbolic pairs. Thus
\[
Q(\alpha)=Q(\beta)=Q(\gamma)=Q(\delta)=0,
\qquad
p(\alpha,\beta)=p(\gamma,\delta)=1,
\]
and all the other pairings among these vectors are zero. Set
\[
z_1=\gamma+\delta,\qquad
z_2=\beta+\gamma+\delta,\qquad
z_3=\alpha+\gamma+\delta,\qquad
z_4=\alpha+\beta+\delta.
\]
Then $z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4$ form a basis of $P$ and
\[
Q(z_i)=1
\]
for every $i$. Moreover,
\[
z_1+z_2+z_3+z_4=\gamma,
\]
and hence
\[
Q(z_1+z_2+z_3+z_4)=0.
\]

Consequently, suppose that a nondegenerate orthogonal space $W$ has a
basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ satisfying
\[
Q(x_i)=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
Q(x_1+\cdots+x_n)=1.
\]
Then
\[
x_1,\ldots,x_n,z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4
\]
is a basis of $W\perp P$ consisting of non-singular vectors, and
\[
Q\left(
x_1+\cdots+x_n+z_1+\cdots+z_4
\right)
=
Q(x_1+\cdots+x_n)+Q(\gamma)=1.
\]
Since $P$ has plus type, $W\perp P$ has the same type as $W$.

It therefore suffices to give the required bases in dimensions $2$
and $4$ for the minus type, and in dimensions $6$ and $8$ for the
plus type.

For the two-dimensional minus-type space, let $\alpha,\beta$ be an anisotropic
basis, so that
\[
Q(\alpha)=Q(\beta)=Q(\alpha+\beta)=1.
\]
Then $\alpha,\beta$ is the required basis.

For the four-dimensional minus-type space, write
\[
V=\langle \alpha,\beta\rangle\perp\langle \gamma,\delta\rangle,
\]
where $\langle \alpha,\beta\rangle$ is anisotropic and $(\gamma,\delta)$ is a hyperbolic
pair. Then
\[
\gamma+\delta,\qquad \beta,\qquad \beta+\delta,\qquad \alpha
\]
is a basis consisting of non-singular vectors, and its sum is $\alpha+\gamma$,
which is non-singular.

For the six-dimensional plus-type space, write
\[
V=
\langle \alpha,\beta\rangle
\perp
\langle \gamma,\delta\rangle
\perp
\langle \varepsilon,\zeta\rangle,
\]
where the three displayed pairs are hyperbolic. The vectors
\[
\begin{split}
&\varepsilon+\zeta,\qquad \delta+\varepsilon+\zeta,\qquad \gamma+\varepsilon+\zeta,\\
&\gamma+\delta+\zeta,\qquad \beta+\varepsilon+\zeta,\qquad \alpha+\varepsilon+\zeta
\end{split}
\]
form a basis of $V$ and are all non-singular. Their sum is
\[
\alpha+\beta+\varepsilon,
\]
which is non-singular.

Finally, for the eight-dimensional plus-type space, write
\[
V=
\langle \alpha,\beta\rangle
\perp
\langle \gamma,\delta\rangle
\perp
\langle \varepsilon,\zeta\rangle
\perp
\langle \eta,\mu\rangle,
\]
where all four displayed pairs are hyperbolic. The vectors
\[
\begin{split}
&\eta+\mu,\qquad \zeta+\eta+\mu,\qquad \varepsilon+\eta+\mu,\qquad \varepsilon+\zeta+\mu,\\
&\delta+\eta+\mu,\qquad \gamma+\eta+\mu,\qquad \beta+\eta+\mu,\qquad \alpha+\varepsilon+\zeta
\end{split}
\]
form a basis and are all non-singular. Their sum is
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta+\varepsilon+\zeta+\mu,
\]
which is non-singular.

The result now follows inductively by taking an orthogonal direct sum
with the four-dimensional space $P$. Indeed, the base dimensions
$2$ and $4$ cover all even dimensions of minus type, while the base
dimensions $6$ and $8$ cover all even dimensions at least $6$ of
plus type.
head: environment

label: prop:converse-omega
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:converse-omega}
Let $V$ be a nondegenerate orthogonal space of even dimension $d$ over
$\mathbb F_2$, and let
$G=V\rtimes\Omega_d^\varepsilon(2)$.
Suppose that either $\varepsilon=-$, or that $\varepsilon=+$ and
$d\geq6$. Then $\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Q$ be the quadratic form on $V$, and let $\langle x,y\rangle
=
Q(x+y)+Q(x)+Q(y)$
be its associated polar form. By Lemma~\ref{l:non-singular-basis}, there is a basis
$f_1,\ldots,f_d$ of $V$ such that $Q(f_i)=1$
for every $i$ and $
Q(f_0)=1$, where $f_0=f_1+\cdots+f_d$.

Let $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ be the basis dual to
$f_1,\ldots,f_d$ with respect to the polar form. Thus
$\langle e_i,f_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$.
In particular, 
$\langle e_j,f_0\rangle=1$,
for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$.

For every non-singular vector $f\in V$, define
$\rho_f:x\longmapsto x+\langle x,f\rangle f$.
Since $Q(f)=1$, the map $\rho_f$ preserves $Q$. Moreover,
$\rho_f-I_d$ has rank $1$, and hence $\rho_f$ has non-trivial Dickson
invariant. Therefore
$\rho_f\in
\mathrm O_d^\varepsilon(2)\setminus
\Omega_d^\varepsilon(2)$.

Set $\widehat G=V\rtimes\mathrm O_d^\varepsilon(2)$.
Then $G\unlhd\widehat G$ and $[\widehat G:G]=2$.

Consider the $(d+1)$-tuple
\[
I=(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d).
\]
Set $s=(0,\rho_{f_1})\in\widehat G\setminus G$
and define $J=I^s$.

For $i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, set
\[
r_i=(0,\rho_{f_i}).
\]
The element $r_i$ fixes $0$ and fixes every $e_j$ with $j\neq i$,
because $\langle e_j,f_i\rangle=0$,
when $j\neq i$. Thus $r_i$ fixes pointwise the tuple obtained from
$I$ by deleting the coordinate $e_i$.

For the coordinate containing $0$, set
$r_0=(f_0,\rho_{f_0})$.
For every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, we have
\[
e_j^{r_0}
=
e_j+\langle e_j,f_0\rangle f_0+f_0
=
e_j+f_0+f_0
=
e_j.
\]
Thus $r_0$ fixes pointwise the tuple obtained from $I$ by deleting its
first coordinate.

Every $r_i$ belongs to $\widehat G\setminus G$. Therefore
$g_i=r_is\in G$,
for every $i\in\{0,\ldots,d\}$. If $I_{\widehat i}$ and
$J_{\widehat i}$ denote the tuples obtained by deleting the $i$-th
coordinate, then
$$
I_{\widehat i}^{\,g_i}
=
I_{\widehat i}^{\,r_is}
=
I_{\widehat i}^{\,s}
=
J_{\widehat i}.
$$
Therefore, $
I\sim_d J.$

We claim that $I$ and $J$ are not $G$-conjugate. Suppose that
$(v,A)\in G$ maps $I$ to $J$. Since the first coordinate of both
tuples is $0$, we have $v=0$. Moreover, $e_jA=e_j\rho_{f_1}$,
for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$. Since $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ is a basis,
this implies  $A=\rho_{f_1}$.
However,  $\rho_{f_1}\notin\Omega_d^\varepsilon(2)$,
a contradiction. Hence $ I\not\sim_{d+1}J$.

It follows that $\mathrm{RC}(G)\geq d+1$. The general upper bound
$\mathrm{RC}(G)\leq d+1$ gives $\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+1$.
head: environment

label: prop:converse-alternating
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:converse-alternating}
Let $d\geq 2$ be even, let $m\in\{d+1,d+2\}$, and let $G_0$ be the
natural image of $\mathrm{Alt}(m)$ on the fully deleted permutation module
$V$ over $\mathbb F_2$. Set 
$G=V\rtimes G_0$.
Then  $\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+1$.
head: environment

label: eq:dual-z0
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E=\mathbb F_2^m$, with standard basis
$f_1,\ldots,f_m$, and set
\[
E_0=
\left\{
\sum_{i=1}^m x_if_i\in E
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
\sum_{i=1}^m x_i=0
\right\}.
\]
When $m=d+1$, we identify $V$ with $E_0$. When
$m=d+2$, we identify $V$ with $E_0/\langle f_1+\cdots+f_m\rangle$.
In both cases, we denote by $\overline{x}$ the vector of $V$
corresponding to $x\in E_0$.

The usual scalar product on $E$ induces a nondegenerate alternating
bilinear form on $V$, which we denote by $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$.
For distinct $a,b\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, set $
z_{a,b}=\overline{f_a+f_b}$.
The transposition $(a\,b)$ induces on $V$ the transvection 
$\tau_{a,b}:x\longmapsto
x+\langle x,z_{a,b}\rangle z_{a,b}$.


For every $i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, set $z_i=z_{i,i+1}
=
\overline{f_i+f_{i+1}}$.
The vectors $z_1,\ldots,z_d$ form a basis of $V$.

Set $z_0=z_1+\cdots+z_d$.
The intermediate terms cancel, and therefore $z_0=\overline{f_1+f_{d+1}}$.
In particular, $z_0$ is also the direction of a transvection induced
by a transposition.

Let $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ be the basis of $V$ dual to
$z_1,\ldots,z_d$ with respect to $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$. Thus
$\langle e_i,z_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$.
Since $z_0=z_1+\cdots+z_d$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dual-z0}
\langle e_j,z_0\rangle=1
\end{equation}
for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$.

Let $\widehat G_0$ be the natural image of $\mathrm{Sym}(m)$ on $V$,
and set $\widehat G=V\rtimes\widehat G_0$.
The kernel of the action of $\mathrm{Sym}(m)$ on $V$ is contained in
$\mathrm{Alt}(m)$. Indeed, the action is faithful except when $m=4$,
in which case its kernel is the Klein four group. Therefore, $G\unlhd\widehat G$  and $[\widehat G:G]=2$.
In particular, the image of every transposition belongs to
$\widehat G_0\setminus G_0$.

For $i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let $\tau_i$ be the transvection induced by
the transposition $(i\,\,i+1)$, so that
$x\tau_i=x+\langle x,z_i\rangle z_i$.
Let $\tau_0$ be the transvection induced by the transposition
$(1\,\,d+1)$, so that $x\tau_0=x+\langle x,z_0\rangle z_0$.

Consider the $(d+1)$-tuple
\[
I=(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d).
\]
Set $s=(0,\tau_1)\in\widehat G\setminus G$
and define $J=I^s$.

For $i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, set $r_i=(0,\tau_i)$.
If $j\neq i$, then
\[
e_j^{r_i}
=
e_j+\langle e_j,z_i\rangle z_i
=
e_j.
\]
Moreover, $r_i$ fixes $0$. Thus $r_i$ fixes pointwise the tuple
obtained from $I$ by deleting the entry $e_i$.

For the coordinate containing $0$, set $r_0=(z_0,\tau_0)$.
By~\eqref{eq:dual-z0}, for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$ we have
\[
e_j^{r_0}
=
e_j+\langle e_j,z_0\rangle z_0+z_0
=
e_j+z_0+z_0
=
e_j.
\]
Thus $r_0$ fixes pointwise the tuple obtained from $I$ by deleting its
first coordinate.

Every $r_i$ and $s$ belongs to $\widehat G\setminus G$. Since
$G$ has index $2$ in $\widehat G$, it follows that
$g_i=r_is\in G$,
for every $i\in\{0,\ldots,d\}$.

Let $I_{\widehat i}$ and $J_{\widehat i}$ denote the $d$-tuples
obtained from $I$ and $J$, respectively, by deleting the $i$-th
coordinate. Since $r_i$ fixes $I_{\widehat i}$ pointwise, we have
\[
I_{\widehat i}^{\,g_i}
=
I_{\widehat i}^{\,r_is}
=
I_{\widehat i}^{\,s}
=
J_{\widehat i}.
\]
Therefore
\[
I\sim_d J.
\]

We finally prove that $I$ and $J$ are not $G$-conjugate. Suppose that
$(v,A)\in G$ maps $I$ to $J$. Since the first coordinate of both
tuples is $0$, we have $v=0$.
Moreover, $e_jA=e_j\tau_1$,
for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$. Since
$e_1,\ldots,e_d$ form a basis of $V$, this gives  $A=\tau_1$.
However, $\tau_1$ is induced by a transposition and hence $\tau_1\notin G_0$,
a contradiction. Thus $I\not\sim_{d+1}J$.

It follows that $\mathrm{RC}(G)\geq d+1$.
The general upper bound $\mathrm{RC}(G)\leq d+1$ now gives $\mathrm{RC}(G)=d+1$.
head: environment

label: l:Vdecomp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:Vdecomp}
    Let $1\ne T\trianglelefteq H$ where $H$ is irreducible on the module $V$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$. If $T$ is generated by transvections, then there is a decomposition $$V=V_1\oplus V_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$$ where the $V_i$ are irreducible $T$-modules of equal dimension $n>1$ and $H$ permutes them transitively.
head: environment

label: eq:T-decomposition
title: Proof
body_md:
If $V$ is irreducible as a $T$-module then the result is trivial, so suppose not. Since $T\unlhd H$, $V$ is completely reducible as a $T$-module.
Let $U_1,\ldots,U_m$ be the homogeneous components of $V$ as a
$T$-module. The group $H$ permutes these components. Moreover,
this action is transitive.
We claim that every homogeneous component has multiplicity one. Fix
one such component $U$, and write $U\cong W^{\oplus r}$,
for some irreducible $T$-module $W$ and some positive integer
$r$. Since $T\neq 1$, we have ${\bf C}_V(T)\neq V$. On the other hand,
${\bf C}_V(T)$ is $H$-invariant, and hence the irreducibility of $H$ gives ${\bf C}_V(T)=0$.
In particular, $T$ acts non-trivially on $U$. Since $T$ is
generated by transvections, there exists a transvection $t\in T$
which acts non-trivially on $U$. Under the decomposition $U\cong W^{\oplus r}$, the action of $t$ on $U$ is the direct
sum of $r$ copies of its action on $W$. Therefore $\mathrm{rank}((t-I_d)|_U)
 =r\cdot\mathrm{rank}((t-I_d)|_W) \geq r$.
Since $t$ is a transvection on $V$, we have $\mathrm{rank}(t-I_d)=1$.
Therefore, $r=1$.
Thus every homogeneous component is irreducible as a $T$-module. We may therefore
write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-decomposition}
V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m,
\end{equation}
where the $V_i$ are irreducible $T$-modules and $H$ permutes
them transitively. 

Set
$n=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}(V_i)$. Then $n>1$, as
$\mathrm{GL}_1(2)$ contains no transvections.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let
$T=\left\langle x\in G_0\mid \mathrm{rank}(x-I_d)=1\right\rangle$. Then $T\neq 1$ is an irreducible subgroup of $G_0$ generated by transvections.
head: environment

label: eq:common-fixed-space-Bi
title: Proof
body_md:
Clearly, $T\trianglelefteq G_0$, and $B_r\in T$ so $T\ne 1$. Moreover, $T$ is generated by transvections, so there is a decomposition $V=V_1\oplus V_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$ where the $V_i$ are irreducible $T$-modules of equal odd dimension $n\geq 3$ and $G_0$ permutes them transitively, by Lemma~\ref{l:Vdecomp}. If $m=1$ then we are done, so suppose otherwise.

Each $B_i$ normalizes $T$, and hence permutes the spaces
$V_1,\ldots,V_m$. If some $B_i$ induced a non-trivial permutation of these
spaces, then $\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)\geq n\geq 3$, 
contradicting the fact that
$\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)\leq 2$.
Therefore, every $B_i$ stabilizes each $V_j$.

The transvection $B_r$ has moved line $\langle\mathbf{1}\rangle$. After relabelling
the spaces $V_1,\ldots,V_m$, we may suppose that
$\mathbf{1}\in V_1$.
Since every $B_i$ stabilizes $V_1$, we have
$\mathbf{1} B_i\in V_1$.
On the other hand, from the description of the matrices $B_i$ in~\eqref{eq:binary-Bi} and~\eqref{eq:binary-B0}, we obtain
$\mathbf{1} B_i=a_i$
for every $i\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. Thus
$a_i\in V_1$,
for every $i$.
It follows that
$[V,B_i]=\langle a_i,\mathbf{1}\rangle\leq V_1$,
for every $i\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. Since $B_i$ stabilizes each $V_j$, this
implies that $B_i$ fixes
$V_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$
pointwise. Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:common-fixed-space-Bi}
V_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m
\leq
\bigcap_{i=0}^{d-1}{\bf C}_V(B_i).
\end{equation}

Let
$x=\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_je_j$
belong to ${\bf C}_V(B_i)$, for every $i\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.
If $\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=1$ for some
$i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$, then from~\eqref{eq:rank-one-ai} we have $a_i=\mathbf{1}$. Therefore, 
$$
0
=x(B_i-I_d)
=x\left(e_i^\top a_i+e_d^\top \mathbf{1}\right)
=x_i a_i+x_d\mathbf{1}
=(x_i+x_d)\mathbf{1}.
$$
Since $\mathbf{1}\neq 0$, it follows that
$x_i+x_d=0$, and hence
$x_i=x_d$.
If $\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=2$, then the linear independence of
$a_i$ and $\mathbf{1}$ and a computation similar to the one above gives
$x_i=x_d=0$.
Similarly, if $\mathrm{rank}(B_0-I_d)=1$, then
$\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j=0$,
while, if $\mathrm{rank}(B_0-I_d)=2$, then
$x_d=0$ and  $\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j=0$.

By assumption, at least one of the matrices $B_i-I_d$ has
rank $2$. The preceding equations imply first that $x_d=0$, and then that
$x_i=0$
for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$. Hence $x=0$. This has shown 
$$\bigcap_{i=0}^{d-1}{\bf C}_V(B_i)=0.$$
This contradicts~\eqref{eq:common-fixed-space-Bi}, since $m>1$. Thus, $T$ is irreducible on $V$, as was to be shown.
head: environment

label: l:transvection1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:transvection1}
    Suppose that either there exists some $i\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ such that $s_{i,i}=1$, or that there exist distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ such that $a_i=a_j$. Then $G_0$ contains a transvection.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $s_{i,i}=1$ for some $i$. From~\eqref{eq:productshortcuts} and~\eqref{eq:binary-Bi-uniform},
we deduce
$$
\begin{aligned}
B_i^2-I_d
&=(u_ia_i+e_d^\top \mathbf{1})^2\\
&=u_i(a_iu_i)a_i+u_i(a_ie_d^\top )\mathbf{1}
  +e_d^\top (\mathbf{1} u_i)a_i+e_d^\top (\mathbf{1} e_d^\top )\mathbf{1}\\
&=(u_i+e_d^\top )(a_i+\mathbf{1}).
\end{aligned}
$$
Both factors are non-zero since $a_i\ne \mathbf{1}$ by assumption and $u_i\ne e_d^\top $ by construction. Moreover,
$(a_i+\mathbf{1})(u_i+e_d^\top )
=
s_{i,i}+1+1+1
=
0$.
Thus $B_i^2$ is a transvection and we are done.

                             
                                    
          
       
                                       
               

Suppose now that $i,j$ are distinct elements of $\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ with $a_i=a_j$. Then
$B_i-B_j=(u_i+u_j)a_i$
has rank $1$. Therefore,
$ \mathrm{rank}(B_iB_j^{-1}-I_d)=1$,
and $B_iB_j^{-1}$ is a transvection, hence the result.
head: environment

label: l:transvections2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:transvections2}
    Suppose that $s_{i,i}=0$ for all $i\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ and that $a_0,\dots,a_{d-1}$ are pairwise distinct. If there exist distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ such that $s_{i,j}=s_{j,i}$ then $G_0$ contains a transvection.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write
$s_{i,j}=s_{j,i}=\varepsilon\in\mathbb{F}_2$. Using repeatedly~\eqref{eq:productshortcuts} and
the fact that $s_{i,i}=0$, we calculate
\begin{align*}
    B_j^{-1}&=I_d-(1+a_ju_j)e_d^\top \mathbf{1}-(1+\mathbf{1}e_d^\top)u_ja_j+\mathbf{1}u_je_d^\top a_j+a_j e_d^\top u_j\mathbf{1}\\&=I_d+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}+e_d^\top a_j+u_j\mathbf{1},
\end{align*}
so \begin{align*}
    B_iB_j^{-1}=&I_d+u_ia_i+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}+u_ia_ie_d^\top\mathbf{1}+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}e_d^\top\mathbf{1}\\&+e_d^\top a_j+u_ia_ie_d^\top a_j+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}e_d^\top a_j+u_j\mathbf{1}+u_ia_iu_j\mathbf{1}+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}u_j\mathbf{1}\\=&I_d+u_ia_i+u_i\mathbf{1}+u_i a_j+u_j\mathbf{1}+\varepsilon u_i\mathbf{1}\\=&I_d+u_i(a_i+a_j+(1+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1})+u_j\mathbf{1},
\end{align*}

and thus \begin{align*}
    (B_iB_j^{-1})^2-I_d=&(u_i(a_i+a_j+(1+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1})+u_j\mathbf{1})^2\\=&(u_i(a_i+a_j+(1+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1}))^2+u_i(a_i+a_j+(1+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1})u_j\mathbf{1}\\&+u_j\mathbf{1}u_i(a_i+a_j+(1+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1})+u_j\mathbf{1}u_j\mathbf{1}\\=&u_i(a_i+a_j+(1+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1})+u_i\mathbf{1}+u_j(a_i+a_j+(1+\varepsilon)\mathbf{1})+u_j\mathbf{1}\\=&(u_i+u_j)(a_i+a_j+\varepsilon\mathbf{1}).
\end{align*}

The column vector $u_i+u_j$ is non-zero. The row vector $(a_i+a_j+\varepsilon\mathbf{1})$ is also
non-zero: this is clear when $\varepsilon=0$, since $a_i\neq a_j$, while, if
$\varepsilon=1$, then
$(a_i+a_j+\mathbf{1})e_d^\top =1$.
Furthermore,
$$
(a_i+a_j+\varepsilon\mathbf{1})(u_i+u_j)=0.
$$
Thus $(B_iB_j^{-1})^2$ is a transvection, hence the result.
head: environment

label: l:transvection3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:transvection3}
    Suppose that $s_{i,i}=0$ for all $i\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ and that $a_0,\dots,a_{d-1}$ are pairwise distinct. If $s_{i,j}+s_{j,i}=1$ for all $i,j\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ distinct, then $G_0$ contains a transvection.
head: environment

label: eq:non-zero-triangle-vector
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $s_{i,j}+s_{j,i}=1$, for all distinct $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$ and $s_{i,i}=0$ for all $i$, the matrix
$$
S=(s_{i,j})_{0\leq i,j\leq d-1}
$$
is the adjacency matrix of a tournament $\Gamma$ on $d$ vertices. By
\eqref{eq:row-sum-sij}, every vertex of this tournament has odd out-degree.

Since
$$
\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}s_{i,j}
=
\binom{d}{2},
$$
and the left-hand side is odd (being the sum of an odd number of odd numbers) we have that $d(d-1)/2$ is odd. Hence
$d\equiv 3\pmod 4$.


The tournament $\Gamma$ is not transitive, since a transitive tournament has a vertex
of out-degree $0$, whereas every vertex in $\Gamma$ has odd out-degree. Hence it contains
a directed triangle
$$
r\longrightarrow s\longrightarrow t\longrightarrow r.
$$

We use the fact that $d>3$. We claim that the directed triangle may be chosen
so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:non-zero-triangle-vector}
\mathbf{1}+a_r+a_s+a_t\neq 0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, suppose that
$\mathbf{1}+a_r+a_s+a_t=0$.
For every $x\notin\{r,s,t\}$, post-multiplying this equality by $u_x$ gives
$$
(\mathbf{1}+a_r+a_s+a_t)u_x=\mathbf{1} u_x+a_ru_x+a_su_x+a_tu_x=1+s_{r,x}+s_{s,x}+s_{t,x}=0.
$$
Thus an odd number of the vertices $r,s,t$ dominate $x$ in the tournament $S$.
Suppose first that precisely one of $r,s,t$ dominates $x$. After cyclically
relabeling $r,s,t$, we may assume that
$$
r\longrightarrow x,
\qquad
x\longrightarrow s,
\qquad
x\longrightarrow t.
$$
Then
$$
x\longrightarrow t\longrightarrow r\longrightarrow x
$$
is a directed triangle. Moreover,
$$
(\mathbf{1}+a_x+a_t+a_r)u_s
=
1+s_{x,s}+s_{t,s}+s_{r,s}
=
1+1+0+1
=
1.
$$
Hence
$\mathbf{1}+a_x+a_t+a_r\neq 0$ and~\eqref{eq:non-zero-triangle-vector} is satisfied  by this new directed triangle.

We may therefore suppose that every vertex outside $\{r,s,t\}$ is dominated
by all three of $r,s,t$. If the subtournament induced on
$\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\setminus\{r,s,t\}$
contains a directed triangle with vertices $x,y,z$, then
$(\mathbf{1}+a_x+a_y+a_z)u_r=1$, because $x,y,z$ are dominated by $r,s,t$. Hence
$\mathbf{1}+a_x+a_y+a_z\neq 0$  and~\eqref{eq:non-zero-triangle-vector} is satisfied  by this new directed triangle.
On the other hand, if this subtournament is transitive, then it has a vertex
of out-degree $0$ within the subtournament. Since this vertex is also
dominated by $r,s,t$, it has out-degree $0$ in the whole tournament, a
contradiction. This proves the claim.

Choose a directed triangle
$$
r\longrightarrow s\longrightarrow t\longrightarrow r
$$
satisfying~\eqref{eq:non-zero-triangle-vector}.
A direct calculation, using
\eqref{eq:binary-Bi-uniform}
gives
\begin{align*}
    B_rB_sB_t^{-1}=&\,B_r(I_d+u_s(a_s+a_t)+u_t\mathbf{1})\\=&\,I_d+u_ra_r+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}+u_s(a_s+a_t)+u_ra_ru_s(a_s+a_t)+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}u_s(a_s+a_t)\\&+u_t\mathbf{1}+u_ra_ru_t\mathbf{1}+e_d^\top\mathbf{1}u_t\mathbf{1}\\=&\,I_d+(u_s+u_r+e_d^\top)(a_s+a_t)+u_ra_r+u_t\mathbf{1},
\end{align*}
so 


\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{eq:Y-square-original-coordinates}
(B_rB_sB_t^{-1})^2-I_d
&=((u_s+u_r+e_d^\top)(a_s+a_t)+u_ra_r+u_t\mathbf{1})^2                                                                                                           
\\&=
(e_d^\top+u_r+u_s+u_t)(\mathbf{1}+a_r+a_s+a_t).
\end{split}
\end{align}
Both factors on the right-hand side are non-zero. Indeed, the row vector is
non-zero by~\eqref{eq:non-zero-triangle-vector}, while the column vector is
non-zero since $d>3$ and $u_0,\ldots,u_{d-1}$ form a basis.
We now show that the product in the reverse order is zero. First,
$$
(\mathbf{1}+a_r+a_s+a_t)e_d^\top 
=
1+1+1+1
=
0.
$$
Moreover,
$\mathbf{1}(u_r+u_s+u_t)=1$,
and, since
$$
r\longrightarrow s\longrightarrow t\longrightarrow r,
$$
we have
$$
(a_r+a_s+a_t)(u_r+u_s+u_t)
=
s_{r,s}+s_{s,t}+s_{t,r}
=
1.
$$
Therefore,
$
(\mathbf{1}+a_r+a_s+a_t)(e_d^\top +u_r+u_s+u_t)=0$.
It follows from~\eqref{eq:Y-square-original-coordinates} that $(B_rB_sB_t^{-1})^2$ is a
transvection.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $T=\left\langle x\in G_0\mid \mathrm{rank}(x-I_d)=1\right\rangle.$ Then $T\ne 1$ is an irreducible subgroup of $G_0$ generated by transvections.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemmas~\ref{l:transvection1},~\ref{l:transvections2}, and~\ref{l:transvection3}, $T\ne 1$. Moreover, it is clear that $T\unlhd G_0$. Suppose that $T$ is not irreducible. Then by Lemma~\ref{l:Vdecomp} there exists a decomposition
$$
V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m
$$
into irreducible $T$-modules of the same odd dimension $n\geq 3$, where
$m>1$, and $G_0$ permutes the spaces $V_1,\ldots,V_m$ transitively. Since
$\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=2<n$,
each $B_i$ stabilizes every $V_j$.
For $i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$, the linear independence of $a_i$ and $\mathbf{1}$
gives
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_i)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_je_j\in V
:
x_i=x_d=0
\right\}.
$$
Since every $B_i$ stabilizes each $V_j$, every ${\bf C}_V(B_i)$ is decomposable with
respect to $V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$, that is, ${\bf C}_V(B_i)=\bigoplus_j{\bf C}_{V_j}(B_i)$.

Now set
$F=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}\rangle$.
We have
$$
F=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}{\bf C}_V(B_i),
$$
and, for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$,
$$
\langle e_j\rangle
=
\bigcap_{\substack{1\leq i\leq d-1\\i\neq j}}{\bf C}_V(B_i).
$$
Thus $F$ and each line $\langle e_j\rangle$ are decomposable with respect to $V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$, that is, $F=\bigoplus_k(F\cap V_k)$ and $\langle e_j\rangle=\bigoplus_k(\langle e_j\rangle\cap V_k)$. In particular,
each $e_j$ belongs to exactly one of the spaces $V_1,\ldots,V_m$.

Set
$F_k=F\cap V_k$.
Then $
F=F_1\oplus\cdots\oplus F_m$.
Since $F$ has codimension $1$ in $V$, all but one of the spaces $F_k$ are
equal to $V_k$, while the remaining one has codimension $1$ in the
corresponding $V_k$. In particular,
$F_k\neq 0$, for every $k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. In fact, each $F_k$ contains at least one of the vectors
$e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}$. Indeed, every $e_j$ belongs to one of the
summands $V_k$, and the vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}$ form a basis of
$F$. More explicitly,
$$
F\cap V_k=
\left\langle
e_j\mid e_j\in V_k
\right\rangle.
$$

On the other hand, the linear independence of $a_0$ and $\mathbf{1}$ gives
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_0)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_je_j\in F
 :\
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j=0
\right\}.
$$
Let $\varphi:F\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2$
be the linear map defined by
$\varphi(e_j)=1$, for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$.
Then  ${\bf C}_V(B_0)=\ker(\varphi)$.

Since $B_0$ stabilizes every $V_k$, the space ${\bf C}_V(B_0)$ is decomposable
with respect to
$F=F_1\oplus\cdots\oplus F_m$.
A decomposable subspace of codimension $1$ in $F$ contains $F_k$ for all
but one value of $k$. On the other hand, since each $F_k$ contains some $e_j$ we deduce that
$\varphi|_{F_k}\neq 0$ for all $k$.
Thus no $F_k$ is contained in $\ker(\varphi)$, a contradiction, whence $T$ is irreducible.
head: environment

label: l:ainot0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:ainot0}
    Let $i\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$. Then $a_i\ne 0$ and $\delta\in\mathrm{Im}(B_i-I_d).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that some $a_i=0$. Then $(t_i,B_i)=(0,I_d+e_d^\top\delta)$, but
$B_i=I_d+e_d^\top \delta$ fixes
$e_j$ for all $j\in\{1,\dots,d-1\}$, and maps $e_d$ to
$e_d+\delta=w$.
Thus the affine transformation $g_i=(t_i,B_i)$ maps the whole tuple
$I$ to the whole tuple $J$, contrary to our assumption.

For the second claim, when
$i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$, this follows from
$e_d(B_i-I_d)=\delta$.
For $i=0$, observe that
$(e_d+e_1)u_0=0$ and $(e_d+e_1)e_d^\top =1$,
whence $(e_d+e_1)(B_0-I_d)=\delta$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let
$
T=
\left\langle
x\in G_0\mid \mathrm{rank}(x-I_d)=1
\right\rangle.
$
Then $1\ne T\unlhd G_0$ and $T$ is irreducible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $T$ is reducible. By Lemma~\ref{l:Vdecomp} there exists a decomposition
$$
V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m
$$
into irreducible $T$-modules of the same dimension $n\geq 2$, where $m>1$,
and $G_0$ permutes the spaces $V_1,\ldots,V_m$ transitively.

For every $i\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$, equation
\eqref{eq:basis-Bi-uniform} gives
$\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)\leq2$.
We first prove that every $B_i$ stabilizes every $V_k$.

Suppose first that $n>2$. If $B_i$ maps $V_k$ to a distinct
summand $V_\ell$, then the restriction
$(B_i-I_d)|_{V_k}$
is injective. Indeed, if $x\in V_k$ and $x(B_i-I_d)=0$, then
$x=xB_i\in V_k\cap V_\ell=0$.
Therefore, $
\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)\geq\dim V_k=n>2$,
a contradiction. Thus every $B_i$ stabilizes every $V_k$ when
$n\geq3$.

It remains to consider the case $n=2$. Since $B_r$ is a transvection, its moved space has dimension $1$.
As $\delta$ is a non-zero element of this moved space by Lemma~\ref{l:ainot0}, we have
$\mathrm{Im}(B_r-I_d)=\langle\delta\rangle$.
Now $B_r\in T$, so $B_r$ stabilizes each $V_k$. Since $B_r$ stabilizes every $V_k$, the space
$$\mathrm{Im}(B_r-I_d)=\bigoplus_{k}\mathrm{Im}((B_r-I_d)_{V_k})$$
is decomposable. As this space equals the line $\langle\delta\rangle$, there
exists a unique summand, say $W$, such that
$\delta\in W$.
Fix $i\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. Suppose first that $B_i$ maps $W$ to a
distinct summand $W'$. Then
$(B_i-I_d)|_W$
is injective, and hence its image has dimension $2$. Since
$\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)\leq2$, we deduce
$$
\mathrm{Im}(B_i-I_d)
=
\mathrm{Im}\bigl((B_i-I_d)|_W\bigr).
$$
However, if $0\neq x\in W$, then $x(B_i-I_d)=xB_i+x$
has a non-zero component in $W'$. Therefore,
$$
\mathrm{Im}\bigl((B_i-I_d)|_W\bigr)\cap W=0.
$$
This contradicts $0\neq\delta\in
\mathrm{Im}(B_i-I_d)\cap W$.
Thus $B_i$ stabilizes $W$.

Suppose now that $B_i$ maps some summand $V_k$ to a distinct
summand $V_\ell$. Since $B_i$ stabilizes $W$, neither $V_k$ nor
$V_\ell$ is equal to $W$. As above,
$(B_i-I_d)|_{V_k}$
is injective, so its image has dimension $2$ and is contained in
$V_k\oplus V_\ell$. In particular, this image is disjoint from $W$.
Since $0\neq\delta\in
\mathrm{Im}(B_i-I_d)\cap W$,
we deduce that
\[
\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)\geq3,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore, $B_i$ stabilizes every $V_k$ also when
$n=2$.

We have proved that every $B_i$ stabilizes each summand $V_k$.
Therefore,
\[
{\bf C}_V(B_i)
=
\bigoplus_{k=1}^m{\bf C}_{V_k}(B_i)
\]
for every $i\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.                                                                                                



Since $u_i$ and $e_d^\top $ are linearly independent, from~\eqref{eq:basis-Bi-uniform}, we have
$$
\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)
=
\dim\langle a_i,\delta\rangle.
$$
It follows that $
\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=1$
if and only if $a_i$ and $\delta$ are linearly dependent. Since both
vectors are non-zero by Lemma~\ref{l:ainot0} and the field is $\mathbb F_2$, this is equivalent
to $a_i=\delta$.

For $i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$ and $x=\sum_{j=1}^dx_je_j$, we have
$x(B_i-I_d)=x_i a_i+x_d\delta.$
If $\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=2$, then $a_i$ and $\delta$ are
linearly independent, and hence
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_i)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^d x_je_j\in V
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
x_i=x_d=0
\right\}.
$$
If $\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=1$, then $a_i=\delta$,
$B_i-I_d=(e_i^\top +e_d^\top )\delta$ and 
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_i)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^d x_je_j\in V
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
x_i=x_d
\right\}.
$$

Similarly, for $i=0$, if $\mathrm{rank}(B_0-I_d)=2$, then
$a_0$ and $\delta$ are linearly independent. Thus
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_0)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^d x_je_j\in V
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
x_d=0,\quad
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j=0
\right\}.
$$
If $\mathrm{rank}(B_0-I_d)=1$, then $a_0=\delta$ and $B_0-I_d=(u_0+e_d^\top )\delta$.
Since $x(u_0+e_d^\top )=\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j$,
we obtain
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_0)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^d x_je_j\in V
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j=0
\right\}.
$$

Set
$$
Q=
\left\{
i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}
\mid
\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=2
\right\}.
$$
We claim that $Q\neq\varnothing$. Indeed, suppose that
$\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=1$. Then $
B_i=I_d+(e_i^\top +e_d^\top )\delta$ is a transvection. Therefore $\delta(e_i^\top +e_d^\top )=0$. Since $\delta e_d^\top =0$, 
we have $\delta_i=0$.
If $Q$ were empty, then $\delta_i=0$ for every
$i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$, contrary to $\delta\neq0$.

Set
$$
U=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}\rangle.
$$
We now prove that $U$ is decomposable with respect to
$V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$, that is $U=\bigoplus_k U\cap V_k$

Suppose first that $Q$ contains two distinct indices $i$ and $j$.
Then ${\bf C}_V(B_i)
$
and
${\bf C}_V(B_j)$ are distinct hyperplanes of $U$, and therefore
\begin{align*}
U={\bf C}_V(B_i)+{\bf C}_V(B_j)&=\left(\bigoplus_{k=1}^m{\bf C}_{V_k}(B_i)\right)+\left(\bigoplus_{k=1}^m{\bf C}_{V_k}(B_j)\right)\\&=\bigoplus_{k=1}^m({\bf C}_{V_k}(B_i)+{\bf C}_{V_k}(B_j))\\&=\bigoplus_{k=1}^m((V_k\cap{\bf C}_{V}(B_i))+(V_k\cap{\bf C}_{V}(B_j))).\end{align*} Write $U_k=(V_k\cap{\bf C}_{V}(B_i))+(V_k\cap{\bf C}_{V}(B_j))\leq U\cap V_k$. If $u\in U\cap V_k$ then $u=u_1+\cdots+u_m$ where $u_\ell\in U_\ell\leq V_\ell$ for all $\ell\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. But $u\in V_k$, so $u_\ell=0$ for all $\ell\in\{1,\dots,m\}\setminus\{k\}$, whence $u\in U_k$. Therefore, $U=\bigoplus_k U\cap V_k$, as desired.

Suppose now that $Q=\{q\}$. For every $i\neq q$, the matrix
$B_i-I_d$ has rank $1$, so $\delta_i=0$ by the calculation above.
Since $\delta\neq0$, we have $\delta=e_q$.
We claim that $B_0-I_d$ has rank $2$. If it had rank $1$, then
$B_0=I_d+(u_0+e_d^\top )\delta$ is a transvection and hence
$0=\delta(u_0+e_d^\top )=\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}\delta_j$,
a contradiction.

Since some $B_r$ is a transvection, while $B_q-I_d$ and
$B_0-I_d$ both have rank $2$, we must have $d\geq3$. Now
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_q)
=
\left\{
x\in U\mid x_q=0
\right\},
$$
whereas
$$
{\bf C}_V(B_0)
=
\left\{
x\in U
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j=0
\right\}.
$$
From this description, we see that these are subspaces of $V$ contained in $U$. Hence, they are distinct hyperplanes of $U$, and hence
$U={\bf C}_V(B_q)+{\bf C}_V(B_0)$.
Thus $U$ is decomposable in this case as well.

For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$,
whether $B_i-I_d$ has rank $1$ or rank $2$, the descriptions above
yield
$$
{\bf C}_U(B_i)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_je_j\in U
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
x_i=0
\right\}.
$$
Since both $U$ and ${\bf C}_V(B_i)$ are decomposable, each ${\bf C}_U(B_i)$ is
decomposable.

For every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$, we have
$$
\langle e_j\rangle
=
\bigcap_{\substack{1\leq i\leq d-1\\ i\neq j}}{\bf C}_U(B_i).$$
Therefore, every line $\langle e_j\rangle$ is decomposable. Since it
has dimension $1$, it is contained in one of the summands
$V_1,\ldots,V_m$. Thus every $e_j$ belongs to one of the spaces
$V_1,\ldots,V_m$.


Since $U$ is decomposable, we have $U=(U\cap V_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus (U\cap V_m)$ and hence
$$1=\mathrm{codim}_V(U)
=
\sum_{k=1}^m\mathrm{codim}_{V_k}(U\cap V_k).
$$
It follows that all but one of the spaces $U\cap V_k$ are equal to $V_k$,
while the remaining one has codimension $1$ in the corresponding
$V_k$. Since $n\geq2$, we deduce that $U\cap V_k\neq0$,
for every $k$.

Since every $e_j$ belongs to one of the
summands $V_k$, and the vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}$ form a basis of
$U$, we deduce that each $U\cap V_k$ contains at least one of the vectors
$e_1,\ldots,e_{d-1}$.

In both the rank-one and rank-two cases for $B_0-I_d$, we have
$$
{\bf C}_U(B_0)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_je_j\in U
\mathrel{}\middle|\mathrel{}
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j=0
\right\}.
$$
Let  $\varphi:U\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2$ be the linear map defined 
by $\varphi(e_j)=1$,
for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$. Then  ${\bf C}_U(B_0)=\ker(\varphi)$.

Since both $U$ and ${\bf C}_V(B_0)$ are decomposable, the subspace
$U\cap {\bf C}_V(B_0)={\bf C}_U(B_0)$ is decomposable with respect to
$U=(U\cap V_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus (U\cap V_m)$.
Thus
$$
{\bf C}_U(B_0)=
\bigoplus_{k=1}^m({\bf C}_U(B_0)\cap V_k).
$$
Since ${\bf C}_U(B_0)$ has codimension $1$ in $U$, we have
$$
1=
\sum_{k=1}^m
\mathrm{codim}_{U\cap V_k}({\bf C}_U(B_0)\cap V_k).
$$
Therefore, ${\bf C}_U(B_0)$ contains $U\cap V_k$ for all but one value of $k$.

On the other hand, every $U\cap V_k$ contains some $e_j$, and
$\varphi(e_j)=1$.
Hence $
\varphi|_{U\cap V_k}\neq0$,
and therefore $U\cap V_k\not\leq\ker(\varphi)={\bf C}_U(B_0)$
for every $k$. Since $m>1$, this is a contradiction.

Therefore, $T$ is irreducible.
head: environment

label: l:G0notransvection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:G0notransvection}
    The group $G_0$ contains no transvection.
head: environment

label: eq:T-decomposition-complete
title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $G_0$ contains a transvection.
Set
\[
T=
\left\langle
x\in G_0\mid \mathrm{rank}(x-I_d)=1
\right\rangle.
\]
Then $1\neq T\unlhd G_0$. We claim first that $T$ is irreducible.

Suppose otherwise. By Lemma~\ref{l:Vdecomp}, there is a decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-decomposition-complete}
V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m
\end{equation}
for some $m>1$, where the $V_k$ are irreducible $T$-modules of the same
dimension $n\geq 2$, and $G_0$ permutes them transitively.

Every $B_i$ normalizes $T$ and therefore permutes the summands in
\eqref{eq:T-decomposition-complete}. If $n\geq3$ and $B_i$ maps
$V_k$ to a distinct summand, then
$(B_i-I_d)|_{V_k}$ is injective, so
\[
\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)\geq n>2,
\]
a contradiction. Hence every $B_i$ stabilizes every $V_k$ when
$n\geq3$.

Suppose that $n=2$. A non-trivial cycle of length $\ell$ on the blocks
contributes at least $2(\ell-1)$ to the rank of $B_i-I_d$. Thus the permutation
induced by a matrix $B_i$ on the summands is either trivial or a single transposition.                                   
                                                     
                                    
               
                                
                                                                
                             
Assume that some $B_r$ interchanges two summands; without loss of generality assume $B_r$ interchanges $V_1$ and $V_2$.
The restriction $(B_r-I_d)|_{V_1}$ is injective and has two-dimensional
image. Since $\mathrm{rank}(B_r-I_d)=2$, this is the whole moved space.
Every non-zero vector in this image has non-zero components in both
$V_1$ and $V_2$. Thus Lemma~\ref{l:ainot0} implies that
$\delta$ has non-zero components in precisely $V_1$ and $V_2$.

If another $B_i$ interchanges two summands, the same argument and
Lemma~\ref{l:ainot0} show that it interchanges $V_1$ and
$V_2$. On the other hand, if $B_i$ stabilizes every summand, then the restrictions of $B_i-I_d$ to both $V_1$ and
$V_2$ are non-zero since $\delta\in\mathrm{Im}(B_i-I_d)$ and the $V_1$- and $V_2$-components
of $\delta$ are non-zero. Since $\mathrm{rank}(B_i-I_d)=2$, it follows that $B_i$ fixes every other
summand pointwise, and similarly for a matrix $B_i$ interchanging $V_1$ and $V_2$. Hence every summand different from $V_1$ and $V_2$ is contained in the intersection in~\eqref{eq:intersection-Bi-zero-complete}. It follows that $m=2$ and $d=4$, a contradiction to the assumption that $d\geq 9$.

We may therefore assume that every $B_i$ stabilizes every summand in
\eqref{eq:T-decomposition-complete} and that $n\geq 2$. The fixed spaces in
\eqref{eq:rank-two-fixed-i-complete} and
\eqref{eq:rank-two-fixed-zero-complete} are then decomposable with
respect to~\eqref{eq:T-decomposition-complete}. Since $d>8$, the elements $B_1$ and $B_2$ exist and satisfy $U={\bf C}_V(B_1)+{\bf C}_V(B_2)$, and hence $U$ is decomposable. Also, for every
$j\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$,
\[
\langle e_j\rangle
=
\bigcap_{\substack{1\leq i\leq d-1\\i\neq j}}
{\bf C}_V(B_i),
\]
so every line $\langle e_j\rangle$ is decomposable and is contained in
one summand.

Put $U_k=U\cap V_k$. Since $U$ has codimension $1$ in $V$, every
$U_k$ is non-zero. Since the coordinate lines span $U$ and each of
them belongs to one summand, every $U_k$ contains some $e_j$.

Define
\[
\varphi:U\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2,
\qquad
\varphi\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_je_j\right)
=
\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}x_j.
\]
Then ${\bf C}_V(B_0)=\ker(\varphi)$. This is a decomposable hyperplane
of the decomposable space
$U=U_1\oplus\cdots\oplus U_m$. Therefore it contains $U_k$ for all
but at most one value of $k$. On the other hand, every $U_k$ contains an
$e_j$, and $\varphi(e_j)=1$. Thus no $U_k$ is contained in
$\ker(\varphi)$, a contradiction.

Therefore $T$ is irreducible. Finally, applying McLaughlin's classification, and using the exclusions already proved at the end of Section~\ref{sec:subsub4}, gives $T=\mathrm{SL}_d(2)=\mathrm{GL}_d(2)$.
Thus $G_0=\mathrm{GL}_d(2)$, contrary to
\eqref{eq:C-not-G0-complete}, hence the result.

label: l:symmetric-pairing-complete
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $i\neq j$. The product $Y_iY_j$ belongs to $H$. Indeed, if
$j=\infty$ then $Y_iY_j=B_i$, if $i=\infty$ then $Y_iY_j=B_j^{-1}$, and if $i,j\neq\infty$, then $X_iX_j=B_iB_j^{-1}\in H$.
Set $\lambda=v_ic_j$ and $\mu=v_jc_i$. If
$(\lambda,\mu)=(1,0)$, a direct multiplication gives
\[
(Y_iY_j)^2=I_d+c_iv_j,
\]
which is a transvection in $H$. If $(\lambda,\mu)=(0,1)$, then
\[
(Y_iY_j)^2=I_d+c_jv_i
\]
is a transvection in $H$. Both options contradict
Lemma~\ref{l:G0notransvection}, whence $\lambda=\mu$ and the first part of the statement is now proven.

Now $B_i=X_iC=Y_iY_\infty$. If
$v_ic_\infty=v_\infty c_i=0$, then the two transvections commute and their
nonidentity product has order $2$. If
$v_ic_\infty=v_\infty c_i=1$, then a direct computation shows that the product $Y_iY_\infty$ has order $3$.
